title: Real Numbers
prerequisites: Difference between rational and irrational numbers.
Ability to find HCF and LCM by prime factorisation.
Knowledge of divisibility and prime numbers.

topics.title: Euclid's Division Lemma and Algorithm
topics.quick_summary: Euclid's division lemma states that for any integers a and b with b > 0 there exist unique q and r with a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < b, and repeated use of it gives the HCF.
topics.real_life: Cutting the largest identical tiles that exactly fit two different wall lengths is a HCF problem solved fastest by Euclid's algorithm.

detailed.definition: Euclid's division lemma: given positive integers a and b, there exist unique integers q (quotient) and r (remainder) such that a = bq + r, where 0 ≤ r < b. The division algorithm applies this repeatedly to find the HCF.
detailed.key_idea: The remainder condition 0 ≤ r < b is what makes q and r unique. Without it, infinitely many pairs would satisfy a = bq + r.
detailed.working_principle: To find HCF(a, b) with a > b, divide a by b, then divide b by the remainder, and continue. The last non-zero remainder is the HCF.
applications: Any positive odd integer can be written as 6q + 1, 6q + 3 or 6q + 5.
The square of any positive integer is of the form 3m or 3m + 1.
HCF(455, 42) = 7 by three steps of the algorithm.

points: a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b; q and r are unique.
Euclid's algorithm: the last non-zero remainder is the HCF.
The lemma is used to prove general statements about the form of integers.
Every integer is of the form 2q or 2q + 1 (even or odd).
The algorithm always terminates because remainders strictly decrease.
mistakes: Allowing r = b or r > b; the remainder must be strictly less than the divisor.
Taking the last remainder (zero) as the HCF instead of the last non-zero one.
Applying the lemma with b = 0, which is not permitted.
topics.memory_hook: 'Divide, take the remainder, divide again — the last non-zero remainder is the HCF.'
topics.advanced: Euclid's algorithm is one of the oldest algorithms still in daily use and runs in logarithmic time. It underpins modular arithmetic and therefore RSA encryption — ancient mathematics securing modern banking.

formulas.name: Euclid's Division Lemma
formulas.variables: a = dividend, b = divisor (b > 0), q = quotient, r = remainder.
formulas.when_to_use: To find HCF, or to prove that integers take particular forms.
formulas.common_mistakes: Forgetting the constraint on r, which destroys uniqueness.
formulas.shortcut: Repeat until the remainder is zero; the previous remainder is the HCF.

topics.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and Irrationality
topics.quick_summary: Every composite number factorises uniquely into primes, and this uniqueness is what proves numbers such as √2 to be irrational.
topics.real_life: The unique prime factorisation of large numbers is exactly what makes RSA encryption secure — factorising is easy to check but hard to do.

detailed.definition: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic states that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors.
detailed.key_idea: Uniqueness is the powerful part. It guarantees that if a prime divides a², it must divide a — the single step on which every irrationality proof in this chapter depends.
detailed.working_principle: To prove √2 irrational, assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms, square to get p² = 2q², deduce that 2 divides p, substitute, deduce that 2 divides q, and contradict the assumption that p/q was in lowest terms.
applications: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers, for two numbers only.
A rational p/q in lowest terms has a terminating decimal exactly when q = 2ⁿ5ᵐ.
Proof by contradiction is the standard method for irrationality.

points: Every composite number has a unique prime factorisation.
HCF = product of the smallest powers of common primes.
LCM = product of the greatest powers of all primes involved.
HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b — valid for TWO numbers only.
p/q terminates if and only if the denominator in lowest terms is 2ⁿ5ᵐ.
mistakes: Applying HCF × LCM = product to three numbers, where it fails.
Omitting the 'lowest terms' condition when testing for a terminating decimal.
Assuming the sum of two irrationals is always irrational.
topics.memory_hook: 'HCF takes the smallest powers, LCM takes the biggest' — and their product is the product of the numbers.
topics.advanced: Unique factorisation fails in some larger number systems. In the ring of numbers a + b√−5, the number 6 factorises in two genuinely different ways — which is why the theorem is 'fundamental' rather than obvious.
